You must be wondering how this game is related to today’s post on the Master-Detail UI Pattern.

For the uninitiated, a master-detail UI pattern is a design interface mainly used to present the list of items and their details. If you observe, in this table, the alphabets are the list of items and their corresponding details are the name, place, animal, and thing. In short, alphabets are master entities, and each of the alphabets has related details. A basic old world example of Master-Detail UI!

Now let us consider a real-world example. Every one of us uses some e-mail client or the other. For example, if you use Microsoft Outlook, you can see the list of your e-mail messages in one area. You can click each of these messages, and you can read the message details next to your message header. In your e-mail message, you can do any action that you require and switch back to the area listing all e-mail messages.
Here, the list of e-mail messages are the examples of Master and their corresponding messages as Detail.

In this post, I will discuss the Master-Detail detail design pattern strictly from the perspective of web applications. However, you can implement this design for enterprise applications too, but for the sake of keeping the scope focused, I will restrict the post to web applications only. The intention of this post is to understand the basics of Master-Detail design at a high-level using some real-world examples.

## What is a Master-Detail Design Pattern?

You already got a basic idea of what is a Master-detail design pattern. Now, let us get into more details. A Master-detail design is a type of UI design that has a master view and a detail view.

The master view displays a master list of items. When you click the item in the master list, then you can see the details of the item in the detail view.

# The Master—Detail Interface Pattern

[Andre Garzia](https://appli.io/author/andre/) _March 21, 2023_

The _Master—Detail Interface Pattern_ is a tried-and-true design pattern used to create thousands of database-driven applications for many decades. It is so common that once we explain it here in this blog post, you’ll start noticing it everywhere. It might be the most common interface pattern in existence today, and that is for a good reason: it works.

At its heart, this pattern is a way to present a list of records and enable the user to manage them with ease. It usually comprises two screens: one is the master list of records and the other is used to display extended data about a single record.

The reason this pattern stayed so popular through the various computing revolutions is because it adapts well to any screen size.
On a small mobile screen, you can have the master list dominate the most of the screen and then navigate the user to a detail screen when needed. On larger monitors such as a desktop or a tablet in landscape orientation, one can instead divide a screen into two regions, one with the list and another with the details and thus making the best use of the larger real estate.

You may recognize this pattern from your eMail client. They normally show a list of emails and let you quickly select one and see all of it in a detail region.

[](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Geary_v3.32_screenshot.png)

Email client screenshot by Geary contributors, English Wikipedia contributors, CC BY-SA 3.0

Whenever you need to create an application to handle a list of database records, you can go with the Master—Detail pattern and refine it as the app grows. Not only it is a proven pattern, but users are already familiar with since it has been in use and quite common since the 80s.

...

If your application is some form of data collecting application that is used to populate and manage a database — something that Appli excels at — then the Master—Detail Interface Pattern is an easy way to design your software. Start with that pattern and expand upon it as your needs change and your users give you feedback.

Your next step should be to double check the applications you use the most, both on your computer and on your mobile devices. How many of them use that pattern? What extra features they build around those screens that would also make sense for your app?

Hope this simple blog post gave you some foundation for thinking about your application screens. When you end up building an app using this pattern, please share some screenshots and feedback on our [forums](https://forums.appli.io/) . A community is only as strong as the relationships built among its members. A rising tide raises all the boats. Good luck with your app.

You'll learn how to define an AI agent's goals, add tools, and configure its inputs and outputs.

For foundational concepts, see About AI Agents . For best practices, see Best Practices for Designing AI Agents .

## Before you begin: Prepare your tools and actions

AI agents rely on existing Appian design objects—called **tools** —to access data, trigger processes, call other AI agents, or retrieve context. AI agents can also use external tools hosted on MCP servers .

To ensure your AI agent runs smoothly, make sure the following are ready before you start building an AI agent.

### 1\. Prepare process models

If your AI agent will **perform actions** (for example, create or update records), you'll need at least one process model configured as a tool.

* Use a clear, focused process that performs a single task without calling child processes.
* Include a **record type input** configured with a specific record type (not a process variable) if the AI agent needs to write to records.
* Add a **Write Records** node to the process model when the AI agent must create or update data.
* Avoid using multiple Write Records nodes for different record types in one process model.
* If you're using AI DocCenter, prepare a process model that calls the AIDC extraction process. You may need a lookup rule to find the appropriate extraction model key . You cannot add an AI skill directly as a tool.
* Avoid overlapping, similarly-named tools as this can confuse the AI agent.
* If your AI agent will collaborate with other AI agents, you can add those AI agents directly as tools without needing to wrap them in a process model.

**Note:** AI agents use Appian-managed AI models and do not support models in customer provided AWS accounts.

**Tip:**

* Keep deterministic or rule-based logic (such as conditional flows, validations, or calculations) inside the process model itself, and let the AI agent handle only the reasoning or decision steps.
* AI agent's document tools are best for reading or retrieving context, not for trained extraction/classification. Use AI DocCenter models if your use case requires high accuracy data extraction or classification. For document processing guidance, see Working with Documents in AI Agents .

### 2\. Prepare record types, rules, or documents

If your AI agent will retrieve or reference data, prepare tools that provide structured or contextual information:

* **Record types:** The AI agent can only query one record type at a time. Related or aggregated queries must be handled in an expression rule .
* **Expression rules:** Create expression rules to store custom queries or logic.
* **Documents and Folders:** Upload supported text-based files ( `.pdf` , `.docx` , `.csv` , `.txt` , etc.) to Appian. For guidance on choosing the right document strategy for your use case, see Working with Documents in AI Agents .

### 3\. Check access and naming
Ensure your AI agent can access its tools and that naming conventions support clear interpretation:

* Verify that the initiator of the AI agent has at least **Viewer** permission to all connected tools and their underlying objects.
* Use clear, descriptive tool names and input labels. For example, use `budgetRequestRecord` instead of `record` .
* Search for existing design objects before creating new tools to avoid duplicates.

**Tip:** When naming tools and inputs, use concise, action-oriented terms that describe their purpose. This helps the AI agent interpret data more accurately.

### 4\. Keep it simple

Start small by assigning only the tools the AI agent truly needs. Most AI agents perform best with fewer than 15 tools. Once you've tested and confirmed your AI agent works well, you can always add more tools later.

**Tip:** Begin with one AI agent and a few tools. Once it performs well, you can combine multiple AI agents or add additional tools for broader workflows.
AI agents excel at cross-system orchestration. If your use case requires gathering data from multiple sources (CRM, support system, analytics platform) and taking action based on the combined context, AI agents can handle this complexity more effectively than traditional process models with complex branching logic.

**Next:** Create and configure an AI agent to define its goals, add tools, and set up inputs and outputs.

For more detail on tool behavior and limitations, see AI Agent Reference .

## Create an AI agent

Create an AI agent that automates processes based on your instructions. To speed up configuration, you can add existing tools or build new ones directly during setup.

To add a new AI agent:

1. In the **Build** view, click **NEW > AI Agent** .  
   The New menu in the Build view with AI Agent highlighted.
2. Configure the following properties:
   
   |Property |Description |
   | --- | --- |
   |**Name** |Enter a name that follows the recommended naming standard. |
|**Description** |(Optional) Enter a brief description. This description is only used to help you identify what this AI agent does. |
   |**Agent Type** |Select the type of AI agent to create. Choose **Process Agent** to automate routine tasks without interruption, or **Chat Agent** to engage users through natural conversation as a virtual assistant. |
3. Click **CREATE** .
4. Enter **Instructions** that give the AI agent detailed guidance to help it perform its work. You can use Markdown syntax to structure your instructions for better readability:
   
    + Use headers to organize instructions into logical sections.
    + Use bold text to emphasize key requirements or constraints.
    + Use bulleted lists to break down steps or conditions.
    + Use numbered lists for sequential instructions.
   
   The interface displays Markdown by default so that you can edit the syntax directly. Click the **Preview** tab when you need to see the rendered Markdown.
   
   **Tip:**
+ Be clear and specific.
    + Describe steps or conditions the AI agent should follow.
    + Use plain language to ensure the AI agent understands the task.
    + Structure complex instructions with headers to help both you and the AI agent maintain a clear hierarchy.
5. Click **ADD TOOL** . The **Add Tool** screen appears.
   
   The Add Tool configuration screen.
   
   Scroll or drag to pan · ⌘+/⌘− to zoom · Esc to close The Add Tool configuration screen.
6. Select the design object you want the tool to use. This links the tool to the specific object the AI agent will access. The object's latest metadata automatically appears below the **Tools** section. You can navigate directly from a tool's configuration to its underlying design object by clicking the object's name.
   
   An example of a tool's metadata, showing the underlying process model.

In the Empty/Ready state, you can load an existing test case or provide new input values.

To set up a test:

1. (Optional) If you have saved test cases, select one from the **Load Test Case** dropdown at the top of the Test panel.
2. Configure any **Inputs** needed for additional context.
3. Click **RUN TEST** . The **Run Test** button is disabled when unsaved configuration changes exist. Save your AI agent configuration before running a test.

**Tip:** The **Load Test Case** dropdown is prominently displayed in the Test panel for quick access to saved test configurations.

### Review results (Running/Result state)

After you click **Run Test** , the Test panel transitions to the Running/Result state. The Running/Result state displays a summary of the AI agent's activity and a detailed step-by-step history of how it processed the request.

The AI agent test response panel showing a summary and detailed history.
Scroll or drag to pan · ⌘+/⌘− to zoom · Esc to close The AI agent test response panel showing a summary and detailed history.

Tool execution details and agent output variables render Markdown by default. Each output surface includes a tab to switch between the rendered view and the raw text. Use the raw view to inspect the underlying syntax when rendered output looks incorrect.

You can review the history of each step the AI agent executed. Click a step to expand its details and learn what happened in that part of the process.

The AI agent history view, showing details for each step of the AI agent's run.

Scroll or drag to pan · ⌘+/⌘− to zoom · Esc to close The AI agent history view, showing details for each step of the AI agent's run.

### Start a new test

After reviewing results, click **New Test** to reset the Test panel to the Empty/Ready state. The New Test button clears the previous results and input values so you can run a fresh test.

## Next steps

After creating and testing your AI agent, you can:

* Integrate it into your applications by using it in process models .
* Deploy it to other environments using Deploy AI Agents Between Environments .
* Track performance over time using the Monitor tab .

For troubleshooting common issues, see Troubleshooting AI Agents .

# Agent Builder Sidekick

# What is Sidekick
Sidekick is an AI assistant built into the Agent Builder that helps you create new agents and improve existing ones through conversation. Instead of staring at a blank instructions field, you describe what you want your agent to do and Sidekick drafts instructions, recommends tools and skills, and suggests improvements.

# When to use Sidekick

* **Creating a new agent from scratch.** Describe your use case in plain language and Sidekick will draft instructions, recommend tools and skills, and suggest a model.
* **Improving an existing agent.** Open any agent in the builder and Sidekick analyzes your current configuration — including instructions, tools, and skills — checks agent feedback and usage metrics, and proposes concrete improvements.
* **Starting from a template.** When you select a template from the gallery, Sidekick uses it as a guide and walks you through building a customized version tailored to your actual workflow.
* **Turning a conversation into an agent.

You can also manually edit the instructions at any time — the form is never locked.

📘 You retain full control at all times. Every change Sidekick proposes appears as a reviewable diff — nothing is applied automatically.

## Starting from a template

When you select a template from the gallery, you’re redirected to the Agent Builder with Sidekick pre-loaded with that template’s context. Instead of applying static instructions, Sidekick walks you through a conversation to produce a version customized to your needs.

The template gallery is still the best place to discover what kinds of agents you can build. Sidekick makes the output better by adapting templates to your specific workflow.

# What Sidekick can do

* **Draft and edit agent instructions** via inline, accept/reject diffs

* **Suggest use cases** when starting from scratch, informed by templates and workspace context

excerpts:
Product teams, founders, growth and ops teams, and anyone with documents, tools or data they want people to actually use.
If your users today get plain text answers, Agent Builder lets you give them a real interface they can act on instead.

Do I need to write any code?

No.
You can build, customize and deploy your agent entirely from the Thesys interface. Connect your data, write the instructions, and click Deploy.
Every agent is also available through our C1 API, so you can drop down to code later if you want more control. Using the API is optional.

What kinds of agents can I build?

Pick from three starting points:
Data Analytics. Connect tools like Mixpanel, PostHog or Supabase and let your agent surface metrics, drop-offs and trends.
Website Assistant. Drop in a URL and ship a copilot that answers visitors using your site content.
General Agent. Start from scratch with your own data, instructions and tools.
Templates cover common use cases like financial insights, growth analysis, customer engagement, reporting and e-commerce.

Where can I deploy my agent?

Deploy as a standalone web app on a Thesys URL, or embed the agent inside your existing product as a copilot, side panel or full screen experience.
You can run the same agent on multiple surfaces and share access with anyone you want.

How do I add a copilot to my website?

1\. Go to thesys.dev/agent-builder.
2\. Pick the Website Assistant template and paste your site URL.
3\. Click Deploy.
4\. Copy the embed snippet and add it to your site.
The copilot goes live right away and starts answering visitors with real UI.

How is this different from a normal chatbot?

A normal chatbot returns text. A Thesys agent returns interactive UI.
Users see charts, product cards, comparison tables and forms they can use right away. Conversations turn into actions instead of dead ends.

How does pricing work?

Pricing is usage-based.
